extraction.name: CADS-dataset
extraction.description: A publicly available collection of 22,022 CT volumes from 40 sources, with voxel-level annotations for 167 anatomical structures spanning head to knees. The collection includes data from over 100 imaging facilities across 16 countries, diverse imaging protocols, and both healthy subjects and patients with pathological conditions.
extraction.license: Source-specific licenses and terms apply; no single collection-wide license is specified. Source licenses include CC BY 3.0, CC BY 4.0, CC BY-SA 4.0, CC BY-NC 3.0, CC BY-NC 4.0, CC BY-NC-SA 4.0, CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, and restricted-use terms. Users must comply with each source dataset's individual licenses and terms and properly cite the original works.
extraction.creator: Murong Xu, Tamaz Amiranashvili, Femando Navarro, Ibrahim Ethem Hamamci, and Sezgin Er were responsible for data collection.
extraction.citeAs: Xu et al. CADS: A Comprehensive Anatomical Dataset and Segmentation for Whole-Body Anatomy in Computed Tomography. arXiv:2507.22953v1 [eess.IV], 29 July 2025.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: CT scans and existing annotations were systematically aggregated from public archives, medical imaging challenges, focused research collections, and hospital cohorts. Selection focused on scans covering the brain, head and neck, thorax, abdomen, pelvis, and femur, without requiring existing annotations. Additional contributions included manual annotations on VISCERAL Gold Corpus images, 484 anonymized head CT scans from Istanbul Medipol University patients aged at least 18 years, and 586 anonymized triphasic abdominal CT scans from TUM Klinikum Rechts der Isar. Release of the new head scans and scientific use and publication of the abdominal scans received institutional ethics approval.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Secondary Data analysis, Physical data collection, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: Only 4,695 volumes, approximately 21% of the initial collection, contained partial annotations; approximately 79% lacked annotations. Existing annotations often covered only one or two structures. SAROS supplied sparse annotations on selected axial slices rather than dense volumetric labels. Review also identified missing or incomplete segments in existing TotalSegmentator ground-truth annotations.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw sources were volumetric CT scans and available segmentation annotations from 40 collections, including TCIA, Grand Challenge and MICCAI challenges, TotalSegmentator, SAROS, NLST, CT-RATE, AbdomenCT-1K, VISCERAL, HaN-Seg, and other research datasets. New hospital data comprised 484 head CT scans from Istanbul Medipol University and 586 abdominal CT scans from TUM Klinikum Rechts der Isar with non-enhanced, arterial, and portal venous phases.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: 2007–2024; exact start and end dates are not specified.
extraction.rai:dataImputationProtocol: Sparse SAROS slice annotations were interpolated between annotated slices to produce dense 3D annotations for volumetric training. Missing anatomical annotations were generated through specialized-model pseudo-labeling and subsequent quality control and model-flavor selection; available original ground-truth labels replaced corresponding pseudo-labels.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: New hospital head scans were anonymized by applying a Gaussian filter with sigma 5 voxels at 1.5 mm spacing to facial regions. Head-related pseudo-labels were cropped around the predicted brain centroid to remove false positives outside the intended region. Rib labels were refined using binarization, connected-components analysis, and majority voting. Missing costovertebral joints were retrieved using vesselFM predictions, a dilated spine region, morphological opening, component-size filtering between 100 and 1,500 voxels, and assignment to nearby ribs. Final labels were progressively merged from lower to higher reliability, with original ground-truth annotations taking precedence.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images were reoriented to RAS, resampled to 1.5 mm isotropic resolution, and their affine matrices simplified by removing rotation and translation while retaining scaling and shear. For model-flavor training, intensities between the 5th and 95th percentiles were scaled to [0,1] and clipped, and four 128-by-128-by-128 patches per image were randomly cropped with balanced foreground-background sampling. Shape-based quality control excluded the lowest-quality 10% of pseudo-labeled images from Shape-flavor training. Head pseudo-label generation excluded scans with predicted brain volume below 2,000 voxels. Scans were partitioned into non-overlapping training and test sets, with development decisions restricted to validation data from the training split.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The 167 targets were organized into nine anatomical groups. Initial nnU-Net models were trained using existing annotations from TotalSegmentator, HaN-Seg, SAROS, and VISCERAL. Three in-house medical research assistants and a radiation oncologist manually annotated 10 additional structures on VISCERAL Gold Corpus images. Brain annotations were generated by registering HaN-Seg CT scans to the SimNIBS MRI atlas using ANTS non-rigid transformations; sparse SAROS labels were interpolated. Specialized models generated whole-body pseudo-labels, followed by shape-informed quality control and complementary GT-, Pseudo-, and Shape-flavor model training. Structure-specific flavor selection and label merging produced final annotations, with available original ground truth taking highest priority. Medical professionals reviewed all 104 structures in 65 TotalSegmentator test images, classifying annotations as reliable or unreliable and documenting errors.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: MIM software was used to generate some reference masks for the independent University Hospital Zurich evaluation cohort; these were validated by medical doctors. Other cohort masks were directly contoured by radiation oncologists. The platform for manual CADS-dataset annotations is not specified.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Pseudo-label quality was assessed by reconstruction with a neural implicit shape-prior auto-decoder and 90th-percentile Hausdorff distance; the lowest-quality 10% were excluded from Shape-flavor training. For each structure, GT-, Pseudo-, and Shape-flavor predictions were ranked using validation Dice scores, prioritizing out-of-distribution results when available. Statistical comparisons used Shapiro-Wilk and Levene tests, followed by ANOVA, Welch's ANOVA, or Kruskal-Wallis and appropriate post-hoc tests at p < 0.05. HD95 resolved ambiguous Dice rankings. Final merging prioritized higher-performing predictions, used ground-truth proportions to break equal-Dice ties, and allowed original ground truth to overwrite pseudo-labels. Vertebrae and ribs were handled as groups to avoid merging conflicts. Expert review excluded unreliable structure annotations from final evaluation of the curated TotalSegmentator test set.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: The additional VISCERAL annotations were produced by three in-house medical research assistants and a radiation oncologist identified as JCP. Test labels were reviewed by in-house medical professionals. The independent clinical qualitative review was led by a radiation oncologist with 5.5 years of practice. No demographic characteristics such as age or gender are reported.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: nnU-Net version 2.5.1; specialized 3D U-Net models and GT-, Pseudo-, and Shape-flavor models; neural implicit shape-prior auto-decoder; SimNIBS MRI atlas; ANTS non-rigid registration; vesselFM; MIM software for the independent hospital evaluation cohort. Models were implemented using PyTorch version 2.5.1, and postprocessing used TPTBox.
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The data contain patient CT anatomy and information about health conditions, including cancer, COVID-19, traumatic injuries, and other disorders. Source-level geographic origins span 16 countries. The newly contributed head cohort consists of patients aged at least 18 years. New head and abdominal scans are described as anonymized; facial regions in new hospital head scans were blurred to obscure identity.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: Public release of the dataset, trained models, source code, and a user-friendly 3D Slicer plugin is intended to advance robust radiology AI, improve reproducibility, and make comprehensive anatomical analysis accessible to clinicians and researchers without extensive technical expertise. Proposed clinical benefits include faster organ delineation for radiation treatment planning, automated anatomical measurements, and large-scale population studies. The paper also highlights the risk of propagating erroneous source annotations into trained models and evaluations.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: Anatomical class imbalance is explicitly identified: structures such as C1–C5 vertebrae occur less frequently, and some targets have very limited ground-truth annotations. Source-specific training distributions can introduce inconsistent pseudo-label predictions and overfitting. Systematic source-label errors include omitted costovertebral joints and rib or vertebral mislabeling. Shape-based exclusion may remove pathological cases with atypical anatomy, limiting representation of clinically important edge cases. Inverse-frequency oversampling, multi-source training, model-flavor selection, and targeted anatomical refinements are used to mitigate these issues.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: Coverage extends from head to knees, not hands or feet, and finer central nervous, musculoskeletal, and vascular substructures remain incomplete. Automated pseudo-labels can contain noise and inaccuracies; shape filtering may exclude valuable atypical pathological cases. Some structures have limited training examples or ground-truth labels, and very small organs are affected by CT resolution and partial-volume effects. Reported segmentation limitations include an overly inclusive brain mask, under-segmented optic chiasm, omitted superior heart portions, a shortened rectum, trachea labels restricted to air rather than the surrounding wall, and imprecise vena cava delineation. Facial anonymization limits detailed facial-analysis applications, which require complementary datasets or hybrid approaches. Clinical applicability varies with treatment requirements and tumor proximity. Source-specific licensing and restricted-use terms constrain permitted uses and redistribution.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing of whole-body CT segmentation models. Supplementary Table A.3 reports 21,277 training volumes and 745 test volumes, with validation drawn exclusively from the training split. Proposed additional research uses include anatomical landmark detection, automated measurements, cross-modality registration, anatomy-guided synthesis and reconstruction, longitudinal organ tracking, personalized anatomical modeling, radiation treatment planning, organ-volume quantification, and large-scale population studies. Users must follow each source dataset's license and terms of use and cite the original works.
